```{r}
#| eval: true

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(marginaleffects)
library(modelsummary)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)

#Data
swingdata<-read.csv("finaldata.csv")
#Our primary Focus
fastball<-swingdata %>% filter(pitch_type %in% c(
  "FF", "SI", "FC"
  ))
#For Figure 1, makes it so left part of zone is always inside and right is always outside 
fastball <- fastball %>%
  mutate(plate_x_in_out = ifelse(stand == "L", plate_x * -1, plate_x))
#Due to time purposes we decided to focus on Fastballs but could revisit and look at other pitches
offspeed<-swingdata %>% filter(pitch_type %in% c(
  "CH", "FS", "FO", "SC"
  ))
breakingball<- swingdata %>% filter(pitch_type %in% c(
  "SL", "ST", "CU", "SV", "KC"
  ))
```

# Abstract:

Introduction: Generating swings and misses (whiffs) is critical to
pitcher success. Whiff rates are significant indicators of the quality
of a pitchers stuff and the best pitchers in the league tend to have
high whiff rates. As the most frequently thrown pitch type, throwing a
high-whiff fastball is critical to a pitchers arsenal. This study
investigates which fastball characteristics, physical and contextual,
lead to swing and misses.

Methods: Using MLB Statcast data from the first week of the 2026 MLB
season, we isolated a dataset of swung at fastballs. Predictors included
velocity, movement, non-spin induced movement (spin deviation),
location, and count.

Key Results: The model reveals non-linear relationships between whiff
probability and both velocity and movement. Pitch location heavily
dictates outcomes with pitches in the upper part of the zone and out of
the zone being associated with a higher whiff probability. Deeper counts
(2-0, 2-2, 3-1, 3-2) significantly decrease whiff rates compared to
early counts. Additionally, spin deviation and platoon matchups
(same-handed LL or RR) were also shown to be significant positive
predictors of swing and miss.

Conclusions: The non-linearity of the relationships between velocity and
movement and whiff probability emphasize the existence of “the dead
zone”, the point where a pitcher’s pitch becomes significantly less
effective due to being too similar to other pitchers. To maximize
success a pitcher should avoid these “dead zones” in velocity and
movement and deploy their pitch in elevated locations while leveraging
same-handed matchups and favorable counts.

# Introduction:

The ability to induce swing and miss is one of the most valued abilities
in professional baseball for pitchers. Strikeouts have become a huge
part of baseball in the 21st century, and whiffs directly lead to
strikeouts. Since 2008, strikeout rates have risen every season,
reaching historical records in the last couple of years (Baseball
Reference, 2024). As a result, MLB front offices and pitching coaches
have spent a lot of time understanding what makes a pitch difficult to
hit. With the introduction of Statcast technology in 2015, every pitch’s
characteristics are captured by cameras with ultimate precision. Prior
work shows that pitch velocity, location, and movement independently
predict swing and miss outcomes (Martin, 2019 and Greve and Savitz,
2023). Recently, researchers have explored seam-shifted wake, which is
when a pitch's seams are oriented asymmetrically relative to its
trajectory (Smith, 2020). This causes the ball to deviate from its
expected ball flight, reducing the batter's ability to hit the pitch.
Spin deviation is the angular difference between a pitch's observed spin
axis and the axis expected from its movement. Our study uses pitch
Statcast data from the first week of the 2026 MLB Season to model the
probability of a swing and miss on fastball-type pitches in order to
answer the question: What makes a fastball hard to hit?

# Methods:

**Data:**

Our dataset was all swung at fastballs from the first week of the 2026
MLB season (3/25 to 4/1). This data came from Baseball Savant’s
downloadable Statcast data using high-speed cameras installed in all 30
MLB ballparks. The dataset contained 6448 observations of what Baseball
Savant considers a fastball (a fourseam, twoseam/sinker, and cutter). Of
the 118 variables in the full dataset we focused on effective speed (in
miles per hour) to quantify velocity, pfx_x and pfx_z (in feet) to
quantify movement, spin deviation (in degrees) to quantify Seam Shifted
Wake, zone to quantify location, balls and strikes for the count, arm
angle in degrees to quantify the pitchers release, and a binary
predictor indicating whether it was a platoon matchup (where the batter
and pitch throw and hit with the same hand). These variables were chosen
due to their roles in traditional baseball wisdom or in the case of Seam
Shifted Wake, prevalence in recent research. Several plots were made to
visualize relationships between these variables and swing and miss
rates. For each continuous variable we looked at empirical logit plots
to determine the shape and significance of their relationship with the
probability of a swing and miss. Several of these plots
(effective_speed, pfx_x, and pfx_z) showed U-shaped distributions
(Figure 2). To compensate for this and fulfill the linearity assumption
we used polynomial terms for these predictors in all models.
Additionally we made plots to visualize each of the categorical
variables relationships. Figure 1 shows a heatmap of whiff rates based
on location. Pitches at the top of the strikezone or outside it seem to
have higher whiff rates. We also made boxplots showing the whiff rates
for each possible count, and same handed matchups (Figure 1). These both
demonstrated a difference in whiff rates.

**Models:**

We fit several logistic regression models predicting is_whiff (a binary
predictor that is 1 for a swing and miss and 0 otherwise). First we fit
individual models for each variable we looked at. Using these models and
our exploratory plots we then fit a final model with the best
predictors. Our final predictors were effective speed, pfx_x, pfx_z,
spin deviation, zone, count, and a binary predictor indicating whether
it was a same hand matchup. Arm angle was the only variable we we
decided not to include in the final model. Its coefficient in its
individual model was extremely low and had a high p-value, which is also
seen in the flatness of its empirical logit plot.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#Final model
fastballmodel<-glm(is_whiff ~ poly(effective_speed,2)+poly(pfx_x,2)+poly(pfx_z,2)+spin_deviation+ +factor(zone)+factor(count)+same_hand, data = fastball, family = binomial)

#Individual Predictor Models
effectivespeed<-glm(is_whiff ~ poly(effective_speed,2), data = fastball, family = binomial)
pfx_x<-glm(is_whiff ~ poly(pfx_x,2), data = fastball, family = binomial)
pfx_z<-glm(is_whiff ~ poly(pfx_z,2), data = fastball, family = binomial)
spindeviation<-glm(is_whiff ~ spin_deviation, data = fastball, family = binomial)
zone<-glm(is_whiff ~ factor(zone), data = fastball, family = binomial)
count<-glm(is_whiff ~ factor(count), data = fastball, family = binomial)
samehand<-glm(is_whiff ~ same_hand, data = fastball, family = binomial)
armangle<-glm(is_whiff ~ arm_angle, data = fastball, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| label: tbl-results
#| tbl-cap: "**Unadjusted vs Adjusted Models for Fastball Whiff Probability**"
#Format the final adjusted model
tbl_final <- tbl_regression(fastballmodel, conf.int = FALSE)
#List each individual model
ind_models <- list(
  effectivespeed, 
  pfx_x, 
  pfx_z, 
  spindeviation, 
  zone, 
  count, 
  samehand, 
  armangle
)

# Format each model in the list, then stack them vertically
tbl_ind_stacked <- tbl_stack(
  lapply(ind_models, function(mod) tbl_regression(mod, conf.int = FALSE))
)

# Merge the stacked individual table side-by-side with the final table
tbl_merged <- tbl_merge(
  tbls = list(tbl_ind_stacked, tbl_final),
  tab_spanner = c("**Unadjusted (Individual)**", "**Adjusted (Final Model)**")
)
#Dispplay the table with title
tbl_merged %>%
  modify_caption("**Table 1: Unadjusted vs Adjusted Models for Fastball Whiffs**")
```

# Results:

For the outcome variable of interest, is_whiff, 18.6% of swings resulted
in a whiff, while the remaining 81.4% resulted in contact. Continuous
predictor variables included effective speed (Mean = 94.04, SD = 3.22),
horizontal break (pfx_x; Mean = 0.01, SD = 0.91), vertical break (pfx_z;
Mean = 1.06, SD = 0.46), and spin deviation (Mean = 14.25, SD = 10.28).
Categorical predictors included pitch location standardized into 13
spatial zones, count, and platoon advantage.

A binomial logistic regression was conducted to predict the probability
of a whiff based on p the physical characteristics and context of the
pitch. Overall, the model demonstrated acceptable predictive ability
with a Concordance index (C-index) of 0.71. Several of our continuous
variables, representing the pitches physical characteristics, showed
non-linear relationships with swing and miss which were accounted for
using 2nd degree polynomial coefficients. The first was effective_speed,
the pitches velocity in miles and hour controlling for the pitcher's
release point using basic kinematics. The first term of the coefficient
was positive but not statistically significant (Estimate=3.39, 95% CI
\[-2.66, 9.50\], p=0.27) showing that an increase in velocity isn’t
always associated with a higher whiff probability. The second
coefficient was positive and statistically significant (Estimate=8.56,
95% CI \[3.01, 14.04\], p\<0.01), indicating that velocity has a
U-shaped relationship with swing and misses where both higher and lower
velocities increase swing and miss probability. Horizontal and vertical
movement were also fit using second degree polynomial coefficients. The
first term for horizontal break (pfx_x) was large, positive, and
statistically significant (Estimate=19.93, 95% CI \[10.08, 29.81\],
p\<0.01). Because horizontal break was standardized so negative break is
towards the batter and positive break is away form the batter this means
that fastballs breaking away from the batter were more effective. The
second term was negative and statistically significant (Estimate=-7.05,
95% CI \[-13.78, -0.35\], p=0.04) indicating that this break has
diminishing returns. For induced vertical break (pfx_z) the first
coefficient was positive and statistically significant (Estimate=9.41,
95% CI \[1.50, 17.40\], p=0.02) and the second coefficient was also
positive and statistically significant (Estimate=6.72, 95% CI \[1.37,
11.99\], p=0.01). This relationship also follows a U-shape. Fastballs
that “defied gravity” with high induced vertical break were very
effective but so were fastballs with sink and low vertical break. The
other physical characteristic was spin deviation measuring Seam Shifted
Wake. Seam shifted wake was shown to be a positive predictor of swing
and miss (Estimate=0.01, 95% CI \[0.00, 0.02\], p\<0.01).

Contextual characteristics in our model were also shown to be
significant. Regarding spatial location, all four shadow zones outside
the strike zone were shown to have high statistically significant
coefficients compared to Zone 1. These zones were Zone 11
(Estimate=0.89, 95% CI \[0.59, 1.20\] , p\<0.01), Zone 12
(Estimate=1.33, 95% CI \[1.02, 1.65\], p\<0.01), Zone 13 (Estimate=1.68,
95% CI \[1.33, 2.04\], p\<0.01), and Zone 14 (Estimate=1.50, 95% CI
\[1.11, 1.90\], p\<0.01). Other zones that were better than Zone 1 were
Zone 2 (Estimate=0.47, 95% CI \[-0.17, 0.79\], p\<0.01) and Zone 3
(Estimate=0.77, 95% CI \[0.45, 1.10\],p\<0.01). These zones represent up
and away strikes. The worst zones were Zone 4 (Estimate=-0.83, p\<0.01)
representing a middle in fastball and Zone 8 (Estimate=-0.50, 95% CI
\[-1.27, -0.40\], p=0.04) representing low and middle fastball. As for
counts, compared to a 0-0 count, deeper counts had negative
statistically significant coefficients. These included, 2-2
(Estimate=-0.37, 95% CI \[-0.63, -0.11\], p\<0.01), 3-1 (Estimate=-0.55,
95% CI \[-1.01, -0.13\], p=0.01), and 3-2 (Estimate=-0.49, 95% CI
\[-0.77, -0.21\], p\<0.01). Interestingly, the count associated with the
highest probability of a whiff is 2-0 (Estimate=-0.59, 95% CI \[-1.04,
-0.17\], p\<0.01). The other contextual variable we looked at was same
handed matchups which significantly increased the probability of a whiff
compared to an opposite hand matchup (Estimate=0.44, 95% CI \[0.22,
0.67\], p\<0.01).

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "**Predicted Whiff Probabilities by Fastball Velocity**"

#Generate the predictions using Marginal Effects library
pred_df <- predictions(
  fastballmodel, 
  newdata = datagrid(effective_speed = c(88, 92, 94, 96, 98, 100, 102))
)
#Clean and format the table
pred_df %>%
  #Select wanted solumns
  select(effective_speed, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  gt() %>%
  #Make the the whiff rate a percent
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  #Change the labels of the table
  cols_label(
    effective_speed = "Effective Speed (mph)",
    estimate = "Predicted Whiff Rate",
    conf.low = "Lower 95% CI",
    conf.high = "Upper 95% CI"
  ) %>%
  #Center the table
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = everything()
  )

```

# Discussion:

These findings align with traditional baseball wisdom. Velocity is a
strong indicator of a fastballs success and faster fastballs tend to
generate more swing and misses. In our model a blazing 102 mph fastball
is associated with 27.2% whiff probability (Table 2), much higher than
the observed whiff percentage in the dataset of 18.6%. An average 94 mph
fastball on the other hand is associated with a 16.8% whiff probability
(Table 2), below the datasets average. Additionally, it is seen that
higher fastballs tend to perform better. Zones 1, 2, and 3 are
associated with the highest whiff probabilities in the strike zone. As
for movement profiles, high induced vertical break can cause hitters to
swing under the pitch, and low vertical break can cause them to swing
over the pitch. Platoon advantages, a well recorded phenomenon, are also
present in our model.

A more interesting finding is the relationship between whiff probability
and horizontal movement. Not just any movement is good movement for
generating swing and misses, movement away from the batter is superior.
This may be because movement towards the batter is more likely to result
in the batter getting jammed and producing weak contact instead of a
whiff. Horizontal movement also has diminishing returns. This is likely
due to the drop in velocity necessary to throw a pitch with more
horizontal movement. Eventually the batter has enough time to react to
at least make contact with a pitch with very high horizontal movement.
The count predictor also yielded relatively surprising results. One
would expect pitcher’s counts like 1-2 and 0-2 to have the highest whiff
probability (Figure 1). However none of these early count pitches had
statistically significant coefficients meaning their whiff probabilities
aren’t really distinguishable from an 0-0 pitch. Additionally a 2-0
pitch was actually associated with the lowest swing and miss probability
not a 3-0 pitch since 3-0 is the best count for a hitter. This is likely
due to the fact that batter usually won’t swing 3-0 meaning there wasn’t
much 3-0 swing data.

**The Dead Zone:**

The non-linear relationships between whiff probability and both velocity
and movement emphasize the existence of “the Dead Zone”. This is a well
known quality of fastballs, especially about their induced vertical
break, but extends to velocity as well. Fastballs with average induced
vertical break interact with gravity just how the batter is expecting.
They perfectly line up with many of the previous pitches the batter has
seen making them very easy to hit. Whereas pitches with elite vertical
break, either very high representing a “high ride” fastball, or very low
representing a “sinking” fastball are very hard to hit and are
associated with a higher whiff probability. The same is true for
velocity. Fastballs that are around league average (94 mph) match the
batter expectations and are easy to hit. Whereas outlier fastballs with
much higher or lower velocities are more difficult. Especially
considering to make it to the MLB with a lower velocity fastball
requires a better movement profile and command, so that even if the
batter adjusts it is still effective. Ultimately it’s all about avoiding
the average.

**Seam Shifted Wake:**

Seam Shifted Wake is a relatively new pitch metric that was shown to
have a very slight positive association with a pitch’s whiff
probability. A 10 degree increase in spin deviation was associated with
an 1.2% increase in swing and miss probability, holding other predictors
constant. However within the dataset spin deviation had a very large
standard deviation of 10.28. This is partially accounted for by the
several different types of fastballs within the dataset. Sinkers tend to
have high spin deviations than four seams and cutters. The high variance
in spin deviations is also likely due to the data collection itself. In
laboratory settings with much more precise imaging high spin deviations
for fastballs are around 40 or 50 degrees. Yet several pitches in the
dataset had deviations well above these values. This suggests that the
spin deviations measured by Statcast may not always be completely
accurate. As a result, spin deviation within this model cannot be fully
trusted.

**Real World Examples:**

A beautiful thing about Statcast data is that it allows you to watch
videos of each individual pitch in the dataset. Doing so with some of
the best and worst pitches at generating a swing and miss reveals
several archetypes for an effective fastball.

**The Low Sinker:** The best pitch in the dataset was a [Tyler Roger’s
Sinker to Jordan
Beck](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=efd773f5-8b57-3e0e-af1e-5bbed0dbc615).
This pitch (effective_speed=80.6, pfx_x=0.01, pfx_z=-0.86,
spin_deviation=30.3, zone=13, count=0-0, same_hand=1) was a low and in
sinker with a predicted swing and miss probability of 78.1%. It actually
resulted in a ground ball but to an avid baseball fan definitely passes
the eye test as a nasty pitch due to Roger’s unconventional arm slot and
its extremely negative vertical movement. This pitch can be classified
as a low sinker, which within the data set is very successful. These
pitches are thrown in Zones 13 or 14 and have negative vertical break.
Another such low sinker that actually did generate a swing and miss was
[Camilo Doval’s Sinker to Casey
Scmidt](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=280e8c39-720f-3ac6-a27e-63ea3e72580b)
(effective_speed=98.4, pfx_x=-0.63, pfx_z=-0.03, spin_deviation=49.7,
zone=14, count=0-2, same_hand=1) which had a predicted 52.1% whiff
probability.

**The High Ride Fourseam:** Another successful pitch within the dataset
was a four seam fastball with high velocity, location, and induced
vertical break. On of these such fastballs is [Tarik Skubal’s Fastball
to Jake
Cronenworth](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=2bdb6983-7dde-3a0a-91b6-6df4721c77e1)
(effective_speed=98, pfx_x=-0.15, pfx_z=1.46, spin_deviation=51.3,
zone=12, count=1-2, same_hand=1) which had a predicted 57.9% whiff
probability despite being put in play. This certainly matches the idea
of a traditional “high heater”. Another one of these pitches is from the
current best closer in baseball Mason Miller. His [Fastball to Jung Ho
Lee](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=dea623df-c5d0-3fab-824f-9dfe8d7fb0a2)
(effective_speed=104.1, pfx_x=0.56, pfx_z=1.54, spin_deviation=1.98,
zone=3, count=0-2, same_hand=0) had a predicted 43.2% whiff probability
and was a swing and miss.

**The Slutter:** The next successful pitch is a controversial one, a cut
fastball with high horizontal movement. In many cases this pitch has low
velocity and closely resembles a slider hence the term slutter. As a
result many people do not consider it a fastball. One of these actually
comes from Tyler Roger’s brother Taylor. His [Slutter to Brandon
Nimmo](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=19f16b39-802b-315d-9a62-f84596486ff0)
(effective_speed=81.8, pfx_x=0.5, pfx_z=0.29, spin_deviation=9.8,
zone=13, count=0-0, same_hand=1) had a predicted 65.5% whiff
probability. Another slutter more reminiscent of a traditional cutter
was [Kenley Jansen’s Slutter to Nick
Castellanos](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=7a631d87-7cf8-375e-a759-cfed8ae8f452)
(effective_speed=93.4, pfx_x=0.67, pfx_z=1.57, spin_deviation=16.23,
zone=14, count=1-2, same_hand=1) which had a predicted whiff probability
of 55.8%.

**The Worst Pitch:** The worst pitch in the dataset was [Jake Bird’s
Sinker to Victor
Robles](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=e67a2d6c-9379-3fd3-9474-e593b6d75be2)
(effective_speed=93.4, pfx_x=-1.63, pfx_z=0.56, spin_deviation=9.03,
zone=4, count=2-0, same_hand=1) with a predicted whiff probability of
just 2%. This pitch also passes the eye test as a meatball for all
intents and purposes. It is a middle middle fastball, in a hitters
count, and in the deadzone of induced vertical break and velocity.
Unsurprisingly this ball was put into play. Another pitch with a very
low predicted whiff probability was [Michael Lorenzen’s Cutter to Liam
Hicks](https://baseballsavant.mlb.com/sporty-videos?playId=8d1b2992-6d05-3e12-a042-4c9b8941115a)
(effective_speed=88.1, pfx_x=0.11, pfx_z=0.97, spin_deviation=33.5,
zone=4, count=2-1, same_hand=0) with a predicted probability of 6%. This
was another meatball. A middle in cutter at just 88.1 mph that was hit
for a 2-run homerun.

**Practical Implications:** These findings carry significant
implications for player development and in-game strategy. Consistent
with traditional baseball wisdom, throwing hard certainly does help with
generating swing and misses. But velocity isn’t everything and tailoring
a pitch’s profile to its utilization is equally as important. Paring
high induced vertical break and velocity with use up in the zone is
effective. So is a negative induced vertical break sinker or sweeping
cutter low in the zone. Throughout all fastball types, however, avoiding
the "Deadzone" is imperative.

**Limitations:** The swing and miss is not the only way to generate outs
or even strikes. Since this study was restricted to only swung at
pitches it does not account for other positive pitch outcomes like
called-strikes or soft contact. For example inside sinkers jamming the
batter are very effective pitches, but don’t generate lots of swing and
misses so are not rewarded by the model. The model also doesn’t consider
sequencing and overall arsenals which is probably the most important
factor in deceiving the batter and generating poor swings. A pitcher
having other good pitches besides a fastball that the batter has to
consider makes the fastball even more effective. Only having a fastball
allows MLB level hitter to tee off. The final model also does not
consider anything to do with the pitchers motion and release point which
also certainly add to a pitch’s deception.

# Conclusion:

This study sought to answer the fundamental question: what
characteristics of a fastball lead to a swing and miss? By analyzing the
pitch’s physical characteristics and its context, the resulting model
confirms that generating a swing and miss is not simply about throwing
as hard as possible, but rather about deploying a unique pitch profile.

The most significant takeaway from this research is the undeniable
danger of the "Dead Zone." The nonlinear relationships seen between
whiff probability, effective velocity, and induced vertical break show
that average characteristics are severely punished by batters. To
consistently generate whiffs, a fastball must possess outlier traits.
This could be upper-percentile velocity, high induced vertical break
(ride), sweeping horizontal break away from the barrel of a batter, or
heavy sink. Context also heavily dictates the outcome. Even the most
elite fastballs are vulnerable if thrown in the middle of the plate
(Zone 4) during hitter friendly counts. Purposely attacking shadow zones
around the edge of the strike zone and leveraging same handed platoon
matchups significantly amplify a pitches success.

Ultimately there is not single “perfect” fastball. Instead of striving
for a universal standard, pitchers should focus on identifying and
maximizing their own outlier metrics to avoid the “Dead Zone”. As the
game of baseball continues to evolve through the lens of data and
Statcast technology, pitchers are better equipped than ever to
understand their unique strengths and execute pitch profiles that leave
hitters swinging at empty air.
